title: The national review of asthma deaths: what did we learn and what needs to change?
funder: not stated. The article records that it represents the personal views of the author, clinical lead of the National Review of Asthma Deaths, and that the review was commissioned by the Healthcare Quality Improvement Partnership on behalf of NHS England, NHS Wales, the Health and Social Care Division of the Scottish Government and the Northern Ireland Department of Health, Social Services and Public Safety, and delivered by the Royal College of Physicians.
authorConflicts: Personal fees and non-financial support from GSK, Novartis, Teva and Chiesi, personal fees from Clement Clarke International and AstraZeneca, employment as clinical lead of the review from 2011 to 2014, and a grant from Consorzio Futuro in Ricerca, outside the submitted work; member of the GINA Executive Board without payment.
result: Of 3544 deaths with asthma on the death certificate in the 12 months from February 2012, 1414 (40%) were coded with asthma or anaphylaxis as the underlying cause and 900 were selected for confidential enquiry; records sufficient for analysis were returned for 628 (70%) and panels of 174 clinicians considered 276, judging that 195 (71%) died from asthma and that 27 (10%) had no evidence of asthma. Overall management was judged satisfactory in 31 of 195 (16%), at least one major avoidable factor was identified in 130 of 195 (67%), 45% neither called for nor received medical help in the final attack and 77% had no record of a personal asthma action plan. A significant proportion had been prescribed more than 12 short-acting reliever inhalers in the year before death, with fewer than four controller inhalers on average over the same year; avoidable factors related to non-implementation of the British Thoracic Society and Scottish Intercollegiate Guidelines Network guidelines were identified in 89 of 195 deaths (46%).
